Operator:
Good morning, and welcome to the GlobalBank Holdings Q3 2024 Earnings Conference Call. All participants will be in listen-only mode. After today's presentation, there will be an opportunity to ask questions. As a reminder, instructions for queuing up will be given at that time. Please note this event is being recorded.

I would now like to turn the conference over to Emily Carter, Head of Investor Relations. Please go ahead.

Emily Carter:
Good morning, everyone, and thank you for joining us today to review GlobalBank Holdings's results for the third quarter of 2024. With me this morning are David Thompson, Chief Executive Officer; Robert Hayes, Chief Financial Officer; and Karen Lopez, Chief Risk Officer.

Before we begin, let me remind you that some of the statements we will be making today are forward-looking. These statements are based on current expectations and assumptions and are subject to risks and uncertainties. Please refer to our SEC filings for a discussion of these factors.

I will now turn the call over to David Thompson.

David Thompson:
Thank you, Emily, and good morning, everyone. GlobalBank Holdings delivered solid performance in the third quarter, demonstrating the strength of our diversified business model and our commitment to serving our customers.

Our key priorities for this year remain focused on enhancing customer experience, driving operational efficiency, investing in strategic growth initiatives, and maintaining strong capital levels.

Now, I'd like to provide some highlights on our progress in key areas. First, on risk-weighted assets management, we continued to optimize our RWA profile, achieving a modest decline quarter-over-quarter while supporting robust capital ratios. Second, net interest income showed resilient growth both year-over-year and sequentially, fueled by loan expansion and deposit stability. Third, we navigated rising deposit costs amid competitive pressures through targeted retention strategies. And fourth, our efficiency ratio improved significantly, reflecting the benefits of our cost transformation efforts.

I will now turn the call over to Robert Hayes to discuss our financial results in more detail.

Robert Hayes:
Thank you, David, and good morning. GlobalBank Holdings reported net income of $3.4 billion for the third quarter, or $2.10 per share. Our results reflect strong revenue growth, disciplined expense management, and a healthy credit environment.

Net interest income increased 5.2% year-over-year driven by higher interest rates and loan growth. Non-interest income was somewhat impacted by seasonal pressures in trading revenues. We continue to maintain a strong capital position with a CET1 ratio of 12.8%.

Before we move to questions, let me dive deeper into some of these areas, starting with our risk-weighted assets management, which is a cornerstone of our capital optimization strategy. As you know, RWAs form the denominator in our key capital ratios like CET1, directly impacting our return on equity and our ability to deploy capital for growth. Effective management here isn't just about compliance; it's a competitive differentiator in this post-Basel III endgame environment, where we're dealing with output floors, revised standardized approaches, and increased regulatory scrutiny from bodies like the Fed, ECB, and PRA.

As of September 30th, our total RWAs stood at $1.12 trillion, reflecting a modest quarter-over-quarter decline of 1.2%, or $13.5 billion. Year-over-year, RWAs are up just 2.8%, which is well below our loan book growth of 5.1%, highlighting the success of our active management approach. This has allowed us to keep a rock-solid CET1 ratio of 12.8% fully loaded—180 basis points above our target floor—while delivering an ROE of 14.2% this quarter. Our RWA density, at 48%, remains among the best in our peer group; for comparison, JPMorgan reported 52% and HSBC around 55% in their latest filings.

By risk type, credit RWAs—which make up 82% of the total at $918 billion—decreased by $11.2 billion quarter-over-quarter, mainly from portfolio optimization in our commercial real estate book. We've been proactive amid office sector challenges; CRE RWAs dropped 4.1% sequentially to $145 billion, with risk weights averaging 95% under our advanced IRB models. This came from derisking via selective paydowns and sales—we offloaded $4.2 billion in higher-risk office loans at a modest haircut, which also reduced associated expected credit losses under IFRS 9 by 15 basis points.

Market RWAs, at $112 billion or 10% of total, increased 2.3% quarter-over-quarter due to volatility in rates and equities, such as the Fed's delayed rate cuts and the yen carry trade unwind. Our trading book, focused on G10 sovereigns and high-grade corporates, saw risk weights rise to 42% from 39%, but we've offset this with dynamic hedging using IRS and credit default swaps, keeping CVaR exposures stable. Operational RWAs remained steady at $90 billion, aided by our AI-driven scenario modeling, which trimmed 8 basis points off our standardized operational risk charge in anticipation of Basel IV's full rollout in 2025.

On a regional basis, our approach adapts to local regulations to generate returns while staying compliant. In the US, where CCAR stress tests are prominent, our domestic RWAs of $420 billion grew 1.5% quarter-over-quarter on strong consumer lending—auto and credit card portfolios up 6%, with risk weights steady at 45-55% under the advanced approach. We've emphasized low-RWA products like agency MBS and prime residential mortgages, which carry 20-35% weights compared to over 100% for some CRE. This mix lowered our US RWA density to 46%, enabling dividend increases and buybacks totaling $3.2 billion year-to-date.

In Europe, €280 billion in RWAs declined 2.8% quarter-over-quarter, helped by ECB-mandated output floors at 72.5%. We've optimized our wholesale book by securitizing €5.1 billion in SME loans into STS-compliant RMBS, cutting RWAs by 35% through the significant risk transfer framework. Post-securitization risk weights averaged 62%, versus 110% before, and we've seen peers like Deutsche Bank and BNP Paribas using similar strategies to offset the floor's impact, which could boost industry RWAs by 10-15% by 2026.

Asia-Pacific, our growth engine, saw RWAs reach A$220 billion, up 4.2% quarter-over-quarter from double-digit loan growth in India and Southeast Asia. Yet we've maintained low density at 44% by focusing on granular retail portfolios, such as digital consumer loans through our Alipay partnership, risk-weighted at 40% under IRB. HKMA's Basel III adjustments have us prepared, with counterparty credit risk from derivatives reduced by 12% via CCP clearing for CVA RWAs.

Technically, we've advanced on several fronts. We've recalibrated 17 IRB models this year with machine learning on a decade of granular data, achieving PD floor reductions of 5-10 basis points for investment-grade corporates, lowering credit RWAs by $8 billion. We're also piloting Basel IV's revised standardized approach for credit risk on a $50 billion portfolio slice, testing against the 1.25x output floor—initial findings indicate a 7% RWA increase, which we're countering with capital-light fee income from wealth management.

Beyond that, we've sold $7.5 billion in loans to non-bank lenders like Apollo and Blackstone, focusing on high-RWA C&I exposures in cyclical sectors. On funding, our $15 billion green bond issuance under EU Taxonomy supports low-risk weights, financing sustainable mortgages at 25% RWAs.

This all fits into our "Capital Velocity" framework, aiming for 2-3% annual RWA efficiency gains to drive 15%+ ROE through the cycle. We're prioritizing high-ROE, low-RWA areas like retail banking with a 35% target density, payments through Visa/Mastercard with near-zero RWAs, and ESG-linked products benefiting from PRA's 2023 framework. Potential risks include high rates inflating market RWAs by another 5% if the curve bear-steepens, or CRE distress affecting credit migration—but our overlays cap LGD at 45%.

For Q4, we expect RWAs around $1.11-1.14 trillion, assuming moderate loan growth and stable volatility, which should add 20-30 basis points to CET1 and support $1.5 billion in further buybacks. Amid Fed Basel III endgame proposals that might raise US bank RWAs 20%+ per Davis Polk, our proactive efforts create a real advantage.

Turning now to net interest income trends, which remains the bedrock of our franchise, contributing over 55% of total revenue this quarter. Q3 NII was $12.5 billion, up 2.1% quarter-over-quarter from $12.25 billion in Q2, and up 5.2% year-over-year from $11.9 billion in Q3 2023. This is our third straight quarter of sequential expansion, bucking industry challenges from deposit beta normalization and asset repricing delays.

Quarter-over-quarter, the $250 million gain stemmed from a 5 basis point NIM expansion to 3.45% from 3.40%. Loan balances rose 1.2% linked-quarter, led by 2.5% growth in C&I from drawdowns on pre-committed lines after the July FOMC signals eased capex worries. Consumer lending was stable, with mortgage originations up 8% on 30-year fixed rates averaging 6.75%—down 50 basis points from Q2 highs—supported by our refi capabilities in the GlobalBank Home Rewards app.

Deposits held at $1.85 trillion, flat sequentially but with a favorable mix: low-cost core deposits grew 1.5% to 42% of funding via digital acquisition. Our AI-personalized mobile platform, akin to Chase's Sapphire, draws non-interest-bearing deposits from millennials and Gen Z, now 28% of retail. Funding costs edged up 3 basis points to 1.85%, with deposit betas at 45% on new rates, below the 55% peer average per FDIC.

Year-over-year, the $600 million rise reflected 6.8% growth in average earning assets to $950 billion, driven by 9% commercial loan expansion in Global Markets, especially leveraged finance and sponsor deals mirroring the M&A uptick at BofA and Citi. NIM dipped just 10 basis points to 3.45% from 3.55%, outperforming the industry's 25 basis point contraction per KBW comps.

Regionally, US operations shone with 7.1% YoY NII growth to $8.2 billion and 3.60% NIM, leveraging our 65% Midwest commercial share and CRE focused on Class A office/industrial, tested to 250 basis point hikes with LTVs below 60%. Europe grew 2.8% YoY to €2.1 billion equivalent, tempered by ECB caps at 3.25% and soft retail amid 1.2% German GDP, but our UK mortgages repriced well with 4% fixed-rate uptake. Asia-Pacific NII rose 4.5% to A$1.8 billion equivalent on 12% trade finance in Singapore/India, balancing China limits.

Tailwinds included ALM hedging: $50 billion in swaps post-Q1 locked 4.25% receives on 70% of fixed securities at 3.80% yields, avoiding $150 million drag from September's 50 basis point cut signal. Loan pricing at SOFR +325 basis points outran deposit costs, with front-book betas at 35% vs. back-book 60%.

For a lower-rate world, we're focusing on deposit beta optimization to sub-40% via loyalty-tied high-yield savings like Ally's model; asset sensitivity of +$15 billion for 3-5% NII lift on 75 basis point cuts per simulations; and diversification with 12% YoY payments fee growth via GlobalPay Visa, aiming to cut NII reliance to 52% by 2025.

Q4 NII guidance is $12.6-$12.8 billion, or 1-2% QoQ growth and 6% full-year YoY, assuming no recession. Risks like fintech outflows exist, but our CET1 buffer supports flexibility.

Next, on deposit costs and competitive pressures, our deposit base of $248 billion at quarter-end—up 4% quarter-over-quarter and 12% year-over-year—underpins our low-cost funding, with growth from retail and commercial loyalty.

Average deposit cost rose 28 basis points sequentially to 2.47%, and 112 basis points year-over-year from 1.35%, for a full-year average of 2.12%, matching S&P's top-50 median of 2.18%. By type: non-interest DDA at 32% or $79 billion stayed at 0%, thanks to Treasury Management with Zelle and RTP; interest-bearing transaction/MM at 38% or $94 billion to 2.18% from 1.65%; savings at 18% or $45 billion to 1.92%; time deposits/CDs at 12% or $30 billion to 4.35%.

Our deposit beta was 42%, down from 48% in Q2 as we prioritized relationships over volume, better than Wells Fargo's 55% or KeyCorp's 60% per FDIC.

Pressures stem from Fed funds at 5.25-5.50%, with Ally/SoFi at 4.5%+ savings and 5.0%+ CDs drawing $15 billion from regionals per Curinos. Marcus and credit unions like Navy Federal gained share with 50-75 basis point premiums. Nationally, 12-month CDs hit 5.1%.

Regionally: Midwest (45%) at 2.15% with 35% beta from agribusiness stickiness, up 7% QoQ; Southeast (25%) at 2.65% losing 1% share but gaining commercial DDA; Northeast (20%) at 2.78% vs. JPM digital, retaining 92% HNW; West (10%) at 2.32% stabilizing vs. Block.

Countermeasures: AI dynamic pricing with Q2 Holdings cut beta 6 points, boosting core to 88%; Deposit Optimizer rewards up to 25 basis points for bundling, adding $4.2 billion; app gamification reduced outflows 22%; brokered CDs capped at 10%, at 4.75% vs. pricier FHLB.

We're defending our 135 basis point deposit advantage for 3.45% NIM, targeting 90% core via branch shifts and Walmart embedded finance. Q4 costs should rise 10-15 basis points to 2.57-2.62%, beta to 38%.

Finally, our efficiency ratio hit 56.5% in Q3, down 180 basis points from Q2's 58.3% and 470 basis points year-over-year from 61.2%, our best since pre-2019 and ahead of FDIC's 59% median, nearing JPM's low-50s. Trailing twelve-month is 57.8%, better than Wells at 60.1%, closing on BofA's 55.9%.

By segment: Consumer/Business Banking (55% revenue) to 54.2% from 59.1% YoY via 85 branch closures, 68% mobile deposits, AI fraud savings; CIB to 52.8% from 57.4% on 15% treasury fees, RPA cutting loan times; Wealth/Global Markets steady at 60.1% but AUM at $1.2 trillion on green ETFs.

Regions: US (65%) at 55.1% post-AWS cloud savings; Europe at 62.3% offset by AI headcount cuts; Asia-Pacific at 53.7% on digital neo-banking.

Drivers: $320 million Project Horizon savings from Temenos, 14% FTE productivity to $285,000, 42% non-interest revenue. 2024 target below 56% on track; sub-52% by 2026 with NIM to 3.45%, 4-5% loans. Risks like inflation met with $500 million gen AI capex.

We are pleased with the progress on these strategic initiatives, and we remain confident in our ability to deliver sustainable value for our shareholders.

Operator, we are now ready to open the line for questions.

Operator:
Ladies and gentlemen, at this time we will open the floor for questions. [Operator Instructions] Our first question comes from Mike Sullivan with Goldman Sachs. Please go ahead.

Mike Sullivan:
Good morning. Can you provide some color on your RWA management trends and how they position you for Basel III endgame?

David Thompson:
Good morning, Mike. Absolutely, as Robert detailed, our RWA optimization has been proactive, with the 1.2% QoQ decline and low density keeping CET1 well above targets. This derisking in CRE and technical enhancements like model recalibrations give us flexibility for growth and returns amid regulatory changes, setting us apart from peers.

Operator:
Our next question comes from Lisa Chen with JPMorgan. Please go ahead.

Lisa Chen:
Good morning. What is your outlook for NII trends into next year?

Robert Hayes:
Good morning, Lisa. We're guiding Q4 NII to $12.6-12.8 billion, with full-year up 6% YoY. Beyond that, our asset sensitivity and beta management position us for accretion in a cutting cycle—potentially 3-5% lift on 75 basis points of cuts—while diversification reduces reliance. Stable macros should sustain momentum.

Operator:
Our next question comes from David Park with Morgan Stanley. Please go ahead.

David Park:
Good morning. Can you discuss the impact of rising deposit costs on your loan portfolio?

Karen Lopez:
Good morning, David. Deposit cost pressures haven't materially affected our loan portfolio quality. We've maintained disciplined pricing and origination standards, with mix shifts to lower-risk retail and C&I keeping credit metrics stable—NPLs under 1%, coverage strong. Our relationship focus ensures funding supports selective growth without compromising risk appetite.

Operator:
There are no further questions at this time. I'd like to turn the conference back over to David Thompson for any closing remarks.

David Thompson:
Thank you for your interest in GlobalBank Holdings. We appreciate you joining us today. We look forward to speaking with you again next quarter.

Operator:
This concludes today's conference call. Thank you for your participation. You may now disconnect.
